strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use a feasible population-based differential evolution (DE) search over the sample values. Keep the supplied construction as the first population member and as a protected incumbent. Each generation forms new candidates from differences between distinct feasible population members, recombines those candidates with target members, repairs the box and sum constraints jointly, and uses the exact evaluator score for greedy selection.

This is materially different from a gradient or epigraph optimizer, smoothing the maximum, solving convex upper models, or minimizing along selected one-dimensional lines. Its central search operation is population recombination: differences learned from multiple live candidates propose coordinated changes to many coordinates, while crossover and restarts maintain diversity. That may explore basins missed by a single local path, but it is a heuristic and may not improve the parent. The mathematical guarantees are limited to the exact score used for comparisons, joint feasibility restoration, and retention of a valid incumbent. The original problem is nonconvex, so neither DE nor this plan certifies a global optimum or guarantees C₅ ≤ 0.3808.

2. Mathematical specification
Let N be the runtime sample count, Δx = 2/N, m = N/2, and h ∈ R^N. The feasible set is 0 ≤ h_i ≤ 1 for every i and Σ_i h_i = m. For each integer lag k from −(N−1) to N−1, define
q_k(h) = Σ_{i=max(0,−k)}^{min(N−1,N−1−k)} h_{i+k}(1−h_i).
The limits are inclusive and include only indices for which both samples exist. Thus q_k is the corresponding entry of np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full'), with no wraparound; both lag directions and every partial-overlap boundary lag are included. The exact objective to minimize is J(h) = (2/N) max_k q_k(h). Products of h entries make J generally nonconvex and nonsmooth. Do not replace it with circular correlation, a boundary-free identity, or a surrogate score.

For joint repair, project z onto the capped simplex by minimizing ½||v−z||₂² subject to 0 ≤ v_i ≤ 1 and Σ_i v_i=m. The KKT conditions give v_i = clip(z_i−θ, 0, 1), where θ solves Σ_i clip(z_i−θ,0,1)=m. This sum is continuous and nonincreasing in θ, so bracketed bisection followed by a bounded residual correction is a concrete joint box-and-sum projection. Clipping and then independently rescaling is not a valid repair.

For a population at generation g, write its feasible rows as x_i^g, i=0,…,P−1, with exact fitness J(x_i^g). A DE rand/1 mutant is v_i = x_a + F_i(x_b−x_c), using three distinct indices a,b,c, all different from i. A current-to-best/1 mutant is v_i = x_i + F_i(x_best−x_i) + F_i(x_a−x_b), with distinct difference indices a,b different from i and, when possible, different from best. All population members have sum m, so these mutant formulas preserve the sum up to floating-point roundoff. Binomial crossover need not preserve it; therefore project the crossover result before scoring it. The population search has no continuous surrogate: every selection decision uses J on the repaired candidate.

3. Implementation procedure
3.1. Write run(seed=42, **kwargs) at module top level and put every helper at module top level. Use NumPy float64 arrays, math if needed, and a seeded NumPy generator. No SciPy or CVXPY solver is needed. Do not define closures or lambdas. Read initial_h_values from the pre-imported global when available, do not redefine or mutate it, and never hard-code or serialize its entries. Implement the exact score locally; do not assume a signature for evaluate_erdos_solution.

3.2. Resolve the dimension before building candidates. If initial_h_values can be viewed as a nonempty one-dimensional array, its length is N and takes precedence over kwargs; preserve that resolution without interpolation. If the one-dimensional length is valid but conversion to float64 or finite-value validation fails, retain N and use the uniform feasible vector as baseline. If there is no usable one-dimensional parent dimension, accept kwargs['n_points'] only when it is a finite integer-valued scalar in [1,999]; otherwise use N=70. A supplied parent dimension above 999 still takes precedence and must not be resized. Convert seed to an integer in a guarded operation, fall back to 42 if conversion fails, and reduce it modulo 2^32 before passing it to the generator. Ignore unrelated kwargs.

3.3. Implement top-level project_box_sum(z, N). For an invalid shape, non-finite input, or magnitude above 1e12, return np.full(N, 0.5). Otherwise set m=N/2, lo=min(z)−1, and hi=max(z). Perform 64 bisection steps. At midpoint θ, compute v=clip(z−θ,0,1); if sum(v)>m, set lo=θ, otherwise set hi=θ. Set the provisional output to clip(z−(lo+hi)/2,0,1). Compute e=m−sum(v). In index order, if e>0 add at most min(e,1−v_i) to each coordinate; if e<0 subtract at most min(−e,v_i). Recompute the sum and make at most two further bounded correction passes. Bound each update by the coordinate’s remaining room so the correction cannot leave [0,1]. Do not independently rescale afterward. Return the result only if it is finite, within [0,1], and has sum error at most 1e−10·max(1,N); otherwise return the uniform vector. Search code must separately reject a non-finite raw proposal rather than treating the projection’s malformed-input fallback as a trial.

3.4. Implement top-level feasible(h,N), checking one-dimensional shape and length, finite entries, exact box bounds, and |sum(h)−N/2| ≤ 1e−10·max(1,N). Implement top-level score_exact(h,N). Return positive infinity for wrong shape or non-finite entries; otherwise compute np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full'), take its maximum over all 2N−1 values, multiply by 2.0/N, and return a Python float. Check that the result is finite. Use this function for every initialization, trial, restart, incumbent comparison, fallback score, and final output.

3.5. Construct the baseline. If the parent converts to a finite vector and has entries within [0,1] and sum error within the feasibility tolerance, use its values directly as the baseline and first population member; copy for internal storage only as needed to avoid mutation. If it is finite but infeasible, project it with project_box_sum. If it is non-finite or unconvertible but its dimension is usable, use the uniform vector at that dimension. Without a usable parent, also use uniform. Store a separate baseline copy and its exact score as a guaranteed fallback before starting the search. For N=1 the only feasible vector is [0.5]; return it with score_exact and skip population search.

3.6. Set the population and generation budget as follows: for 2≤N≤100 use P=48 and G=180; for 101≤N≤250 use P=32 and G=100; for 251≤N≤500 use P=20 and G=45; for 501≤N≤999 use P=12 and G=20. If a valid parent has N>999, preserve and score its feasible baseline but skip DE search to keep work bounded. These are sequential operations on the allowed single CPU. Initialize arrays X with shape (P,N), fitness with shape (P,), and per-individual F and CR arrays with shapes (P,). Set every initial F_i=0.5 and CR_i=0.8.

3.7. Build the initial population deterministically using the seeded generator. Put the baseline in row 0 and the uniform vector in row 1. Put project_box_sum(1−baseline,N) in row 2 if a finite parent was available; otherwise put a projection of independent standard-normal values there. Fill remaining rows cyclically with these four constructions: project baseline plus σ times independent standard-normal noise, using σ values 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40 in that repeating order; project an independent uniform [0,1] vector; project an independent standard-normal vector; and project a smooth Fourier profile. For the profile, use i=0,…,N−1, R=min(5,floor((N−1)/2)), and z_i=0.5+Σ_{r=1}^R (0.12/r)[A_r sin(2πri/N)+B_r cos(2πri/N)], where A_r and B_r are independent standard-normal draws. If R=0 use uniform. Projection is mandatory for every generated row except a baseline already accepted as feasible. Duplicates may remain; do not spend unbounded time deduplicating. Exact-score every row, set invalid fitness to infinity, and initialize the global incumbent from the lowest-scoring feasible row while retaining the separately stored baseline fallback.

3.8. For each generation, use a snapshot of the old population and fitness for every mutation so updates are synchronous. Find best as the lowest-fitness row in that snapshot. For each target i, independently propose jDE parameters: with probability 0.1 set F_trial=0.1+0.9U for a fresh U∈[0,1); otherwise retain F_i. With probability 0.1 set CR_trial to a fresh U∈[0,1); otherwise retain CR_i. Choose rand/1 with probability 0.75 and current-to-best/1 with probability 0.25. For rand/1 draw three distinct indices from the population excluding i. For current-to-best/1 draw two distinct difference indices excluding i and best when possible; P is always large enough for this rule. Use F_trial in the selected mutation formula.

3.9. Form a binomial crossover trial from the mutant and target: independently choose each coordinate from the mutant with probability CR_trial, otherwise use the target, and force one uniformly chosen coordinate j_rand to come from the mutant. If the raw trial is non-finite or has magnitude above 1e12, discard it. Otherwise pass it through project_box_sum, then require feasible(trial,N). Compute score_exact only for a feasible trial. Accept the trial into the next population row only if its exact score is strictly lower than the target’s exact score; on acceptance store F_trial and CR_trial with it. On rejection retain the old target and its parameters. Update the external global incumbent only on a strict exact-score decrease. A tie does not replace the target or incumbent. If a proposal, projection, or score operation raises an exception or returns an unusable result, retain the old target and continue with the other targets.

3.10. Add a fixed stagnation restart rule. Use a stagnation window of 30 generations for N≤100, 20 for 101≤N≤250, 12 for 251≤N≤500, and 8 for 501≤N≤999. At the end of a generation, count it as stagnant unless the global score decreased from its value at the start of that generation by more than 1e−12·max(1,|old global score|). When the window is reached, preserve the lowest-fitness population row and replace the worst max(2,P//4) other rows. Determine the worst indices with a descending fitness sort, excluding the best row. For three out of every four replacements, project global_best plus σ times fresh standard-normal noise, cycling σ through 0.02, 0.05, 0.12, 0.30. For the fourth, use a projected independent uniform [0,1] vector. Score each replacement exactly, set its F to 0.5 and CR to 0.8, and update the global incumbent if it improves. Reset the stagnation counter after the restart. If a replacement fails, leave that population row unchanged. Run the fixed G generations; do not stop because a target score is hoped for or reached.

3.11. Before returning, validate the global incumbent. If it is invalid, try one project_box_sum repair and use the repaired vector only if it validates and has finite exact score; otherwise use the stored baseline. Compare any final repair against the baseline by exact score so a repair cannot discard the fallback. Recompute score_exact from the final vector after the last feasibility check. If the selected vector or score is still unusable, use the uniform vector and compute its exact score. Return a one-dimensional float array, the Python float exact score, and int(N), in that order.

4. Search choices and useful variations
Correctness requirements are fixed: preserve a usable parent’s dimension and include it as the first individual, minimize the exact maximum over all 2N−1 full linear-correlation lags, enforce both constraints jointly, and accept candidates using only score_exact. The defaults are the population budgets in section 3, rand/1 probability 0.75, jDE update probabilities 0.1, initial F=0.5 and CR=0.8, and the specified initialization and restart rules. Stagnation restarts are the only result-dependent change to the population; their triggers and replacement rules are fixed above.

A coder may choose a different search budget without preliminary experiments: for N≤100, P may be 40–64 and G 120–240; for larger dimensions, scale P and G down rather than changing resolution. The current-to-best probability may be 0.15–0.35, jDE parameter-update probabilities 0.05–0.20, and the stagnation window 20–45 generations for N≤100. Initialization noise may use scales from 0.01 to 0.5; Fourier profiles may use 3–8 modes and coefficients proportional to 0.08/r–0.18/r. Any variation must retain row 0 as the baseline, project every generated candidate jointly, retain a feasible incumbent, and score candidates with the exact evaluator formula. Use the specified defaults if making no deliberate alternative choice. Do not alter a supplied parent’s resolution or claim an untested bound.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
Use float64 throughout, a seeded generator, finite checks, and serial execution. At the supplied N=70, the population matrix has 48×70 entries, under 30 kB; old and next population snapshots and scratch arrays remain O(PN). The full correlation output has 2N−1 entries and np.correlate uses O(N²) arithmetic for each candidate. The default main loop performs at most 48×180 trial evaluations plus initialization and bounded restarts, which is modest for the supplied N. Do not construct a dense Hessian, a lag-by-coordinate Jacobian, or any three-dimensional pairwise tensor. For N>999 with a supplied parent, skip population search as specified.

The projection’s bisection bracket and bounded residual correction are the only constraint repair; never clip and then separately rescale. Reject non-finite or extreme proposals before scoring. A non-finite correlation score, infeasible trial, or per-trial exception must not alter the current population member or global incumbent. The baseline remains a feasible fallback if no trial improves it. All loops have explicit generation, bisection, and restart bounds. The search is stochastic but deterministic for a fixed seed; it has no certificate of global optimality.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
The generated program must carry out parent inspection, dimension selection, initialization, projection, DE updates, feasibility checks, exact scoring, failure recovery, and final selection inside run and its top-level helpers. Check parent dimensionality and finite values before using entries; use a valid parent directly as the baseline when it is feasible, and never mutate the pre-imported global. Check every generated or trial candidate for expected shape and finite entries, restore constraints with project_box_sum, and reject it if it still fails the box or sum check. Keep the baseline and a feasible global incumbent available throughout the run.

For initial candidates, every selection decision, fallback, and final return, compute max(np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full'))·(2.0/N) from the candidate itself. Do not report a DE fitness surrogate, a claimed target value, or an unchecked vector. Before returning, ensure h_values is finite and one-dimensional, each entry is in [0,1], and its sum is N/2 within 1e−10·max(1,N). Recompute c5_bound from that final h_values and return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with n_points equal to the chosen runtime dimension.
